FIFTH-ROUND mock peer review for an ASME Journal of Mechanical Design (JMD)
Research Paper submission. You reviewed earlier drafts of this same manuscript in
four prior rounds (round 1 = Reject-and-Resubmit, round 2 = Major Revision,
round 3 = Major Revision but improving, round 4 = Major Revision and closer to
publishable form); this is the further-revised draft. The attached files are the
current populated draft (manuscript.pdf is the clean reader PDF;
manuscript-todos.pdf is the review PDF that additionally shows margin \todo{}
annotations and a \listoftodos; supplementary.pdf is the Supplementary
Information; sources are manuscript-body.tex / manuscript.tex /
manuscript-todos.tex / supplementary.tex and references.bib;
manuscript/README.md documents venue choice and build).

The paper is a multi-material 3D-printed (FDM) tensegrity-inspired
energy-absorbing structure study using experiment-driven Bayesian optimization
(BO). Rigid PLA struts in compression + soft TPU cables in tension, printed on a
Bambu Lab H2D dual-nozzle FDM printer, characterized under quasi-static
compression and drop-weight impact. The motivating application is framed up front
as a planetary-lander / payload energy absorber; a crutch-tip is mentioned only
as future work in the Discussion. Quantitative Results/Discussion are
INTENTIONALLY still \todo{} placeholders -- the project is at the
planned-methods phase. Please review structure, framing, scope, novelty claims,
methods rigor, literature coverage, internal consistency, and venue fit (ASME JMD
vs. backup Smart Materials and Structures / Additive Manufacturing), NOT raw
numerical values.

What CHANGED since round 4 (so you can focus on the current state rather than
re-flagging already-addressed items). This edit responds directly to the only new
reference ask in the round-4 Associate-Editor letter:
  * TENSEGRITY-ADDITIVE-MANUFACTURING LITERATURE NOW INTEGRATED. The round-4
    editor confirmed all four round-3 citation gaps (SAASBO, TuRBO,
    SEA/densification metrics, SAE J211) were CLOSED and asked only that the
    already-flagged tensegrity-AM works be integrated once verified. Each DOI was
    verified against Crossref and the following are now cited in the
    "Multi-Material 3D Printing" / tensegrity-architecture background (replacing
    the prior \todo{} placeholder note):
      - Bauer et al. 2021, Advanced Materials 33(10):2005647
        (doi:10.1002/adma.202005647) -- 3D-printed tensegrity metamaterials that
        delocalize deformation to resist catastrophic failure.
      - Pajunen et al. 2021, Extreme Mechanics Letters 44:101236
        (doi:10.1016/j.eml.2021.101236) -- prestrain-induced bandgap tuning in
        3D-printed tensegrity-inspired lattices.
      - Sabouni-Zawadzka et al. 2024, Archives of Civil Engineering 70(2):343-357
        (doi:10.24425/ace.2024.150987) -- experimental mechanical properties of
        3D-printed tensegrity-inspired metamaterials (4-strut simplex module).
      - Almeida et al. 2025, Int. J. Solids and Structures 322:113590
        (doi:10.1016/j.ijsolstr.2025.113590) -- high-strain-rate response of
        3D-printable tensegrity-inspired structures.
      - Davami et al. 2025, Int. J. Impact Engineering 198:105208
        (doi:10.1016/j.ijimpeng.2024.105208) -- dynamic analysis of additively
        manufactured tensegrity structures.
      - Wang et al. 2026, Additive Manufacturing 118:105107
        (doi:10.1016/j.addma.2026.105107) -- integrated fabrication and
        validation of tensegrity-inspired rigid-flexible metamaterials.
    (Santos 2023, Adv. Mater., doi:10.1002/adma.202300639, flagged in the same
    round-4 list, was already cited in earlier rounds.) The TODO note that
    enumerated these as "to verify-then-cite" has been removed.

All round-2/3/4 method and framing fixes remain in place: real SAASBO/TuRBO and
SEA/densification/SAE-J211 citations; the primary campaign pre-committed as a
CONSTRAINED MULTI-OBJECTIVE problem (maximize SEA and compaction efficiency
subject to peak transmitted force F_max <= F*, F* fixed from the rigid control;
acquisition qNEHVI; hypervolume reference point at the rigid-control point;
single-objective LogEI kept only as a baseline; robust/evolution-guided variants
demoted to contingency); empirical SAASBO-vs-single-task-GP benchmarking;
internally consistent budget (n=9 Sobol + T=10 x q=5 = 59 specimens); explicit
out-of-scope statement (off-axis/combined loading, multi-hit/cyclic durability,
landing-attitude variability are future work); justified fixed joint diameter
d_j = 7.0 mm; an as-built-resolution paragraph; and a pre-specified Spearman
rank-correlation (rho_s) criterion for the exploratory metal-analog (Al/SS)
transfer test.

STILL INTENTIONALLY OPEN (known gates, do not re-flag as new defects): the
quantitative Results and Discussion remain \todo{} placeholders and several
BO/impact figures are illustrative synthetic examples; some fabrication/test
process parameters (Table 3 print settings, exact fixtures/DAQ) remain TBD
pending the campaign; the Zenodo archival DOI is a placeholder.

Produce FOUR artifacts, in the same style as a JMD decision-letter package:

1. Mock Reviewer #1 -- Design / Mechanical Engineering (typical ASME JMD
   reviewer). Strict on novelty vs. prior tensegrity/lattice/spring-loaded work
   (now that the tensegrity-AM literature is integrated, is the novelty claim
   still defensible and correctly positioned?), on the BO formulation (kernel,
   acquisition, noise, batch/budget, SAASBO justification at ~5 variables,
   constrained multi-objective formulation and reference point), on
   parameterization completeness and Table-1 consistency, and on JMD scope fit.
   Major / Minor / Editorial; recommend
   Accept / Minor / Major / Reject / Reject-and-Resubmit.

2. Mock Reviewer #2 -- Biomechanics / impact-mechanics. Strict on the
   energy-absorber motivation, relevance of the axial drop-tower fixture vs. real
   off-axis/cyclic loading, transferability, and metric mapping (SEA -> peak
   transmitted force). Recommendation.

3. Mock Reviewer #3 -- Additive manufacturing / materials. Strict on the PLA+TPU
   multi-material FDM processing claims, the internal-anchor joint vs.
   alternatives, interface durability/fatigue, FDM repeatability and resolution
   limits for continuous-diameter members, process-parameter disclosure, the
   metal-analog (Al/SS) validation plan, and whether the newly integrated
   tensegrity-AM references are used appropriately (not over-claimed). Recommend.

4. Mock Editor (JMD Associate Editor) decision letter synthesizing the three
   reviews: single-paragraph summary, decision, and an itemized, priority-ordered
   list of revisions required before resubmission. Explicitly assess venue fit
   and explicitly state whether the round-5 revisions (tensegrity-AM literature
   integration) have moved the manuscript closer to acceptance relative to the
   round-4 Major Revision decision, and whether the round-4 reference ask is now
   resolved.

End with a short "Reviewers' bibliographic gaps" section listing any specific
peer-reviewed references the authors are still missing, by topic, given
references.bib (note explicitly that the round-3 gaps -- SAASBO, TuRBO,
SEA/densification metrics, SAE J211 -- and the round-4 tensegrity-AM ask are now
closed).

Be honest, specific, and grounded in the attached files. It is acceptable (and
expected) to note that the placeholder \todo{}s and the absence of experimental
results gate the final decision. Where prior concerns have been resolved, say so;
where they persist or new ones appear, flag them.

Mock Reviewer #1 -- Design / Mechanical Engineering (ASME JMD)

Recommendation: Major Revision

This round is better than round 4. The newly integrated tensegrity-additive-manufacturing literature closes the specific reference gap that remained in the prior AE letter, and the manuscript is now more credible in how it positions itself relative to published tensegrity-inspired printed structures. The paper is also structurally much tighter than earlier drafts: the problem statement, constrained multi-objective BO formulation, design-variable table, fixed-joint rationale, and scope limitations are substantially clearer. That said, the manuscript is still not yet publishable in JMD form because it remains a planned-methods paper with placeholder Results and Discussion, several synthetic figures, and incomplete fabrication/test parameter disclosure. My recommendation stays at Major Revision rather than moving to Minor Revision because the remaining issues are not cosmetic.

Major comments

1. Novelty is now defensible, but only if stated narrowly and consistently.
The revised background now appropriately cites Bauer et al. (2021), Pajunen et al. (2021), Sabouni-Zawadzka et al. (2024), Almeida et al. (2025), Davami et al. (2025), and Wang et al. (2026), and uses them mainly to establish that tensegrity-inspired architectures can be additively manufactured and can exhibit programmable and dynamic response. That is the right use of those papers. The manuscript should keep the novelty claim exactly at the level now implied by Table 1/novelty positioning: not “first tensegrity-inspired printed absorber,” not “first AM tensegrity impact study,” but the combination of (i) multi-material PLA/TPU FDM, (ii) this internal-anchor joint concept, and (iii) an experiment-driven BO loop trained directly on physical measurements. If the authors overstate beyond that, Reviewer 1-level pushback will return immediately.

The manuscript still contains an explicit TODO in the Introduction to “add 1–2 sentences clearly stating the gap this paper closes vs. Pajunen et al. and Mo et al.” That gap statement is needed in the final paper, because the current claim is spread across prose plus the novelty table rather than crisply stated in the main narrative.

2. The BO formulation is much improved, but some modeling choices still need tighter justification for a JMD audience.
The methods now clearly state a constrained multi-objective problem: maximize SEA and compaction efficiency subject to peak transmitted force F_max <= F*; use qNEHVI; anchor the hypervolume reference point at the rigid-control point; keep single-objective LogEI only as a baseline; hold robust/evolution-guided variants as contingency. This is coherent.

Still, several points need firmer justification in the final draft:
- Kernel: the Matérn-5/2 ARD GP is reasonable, but the manuscript should say why this kernel is preferred for this mechanical design problem over squared-exponential or other common choices.
- Noise: the model uses inferred homoscedastic noise. That is acceptable as a starting choice, but it may be fragile if print-to-print variability changes across geometry regimes. The authors should either justify why homoscedastic noise is adequate for the planned campaign or state clear criteria for escalating to heteroscedastic/replicate-aware treatment.
- SAASBO at approximately 5 variables: the current text says SAASBO is retained despite modest dimensionality because its shrinkage priors may improve uncertainty quantification at low sample size, and that this will be benchmarked against a standard single-task GP baseline. Good. But this is still unusual enough that the paper must report that benchmark clearly and not assume SAASBO is self-justifying.
- Batch/budget: n=9 Sobol + 10 batches x q=5 = 59 specimens is internally consistent. Good. But one TODO still says “confirm the final budget against printer throughput.” That cannot remain in a submitted paper.
- Reference point: using the rigid-control point as the qNEHVI hypervolume reference point is sensible and interpretable. Keep this. It is one of the stronger design choices in the current draft.

3. Parameterization is clearer, but Table 1 and the surrounding text need one more consistency pass.
The active continuous variables are R, H, theta, d_s, and d_t, with fixed d_j = 7.0 mm. That is now much better defined. The explanation for fixing d_j is also sound: it is constrained by outlet count and nozzle-clearance/joint-geometry considerations, and keeping it fixed avoids confounding energy-absorption performance with joint-strength changes. Good.

Still, I would ask the authors to check three things carefully:
- The text says the family is parameterized via four groups of variables, but only five continuous variables are active in the present campaign. That distinction is correct, but it should be restated once in plainer language for readers who do not work in BO.
- The manuscript says the surrogate will be fit on realized as-built geometry, not commanded CAD values. That is a strong choice. The authors should make explicit whether Table 1 ranges refer to commanded CAD inputs, realized measured values, or both.
- The as-built discretization paragraph is good, but it quietly undercuts the “continuous variable” framing. I think that is honest, but it means the final paper should explain how measured diameters are fed back into Ax/BoTorch without creating bookkeeping ambiguity between design intent and realized specimen.

4. Venue fit is plausible for JMD, but the paper must stay design-method centric.
As revised, this can fit JMD if the final manuscript centers on design representation, experiment-driven optimization, and the way the constrained multi-objective formulation guides the search. If the eventual paper leans mainly on materials processing, impact test traces, and print-parameter tuning, it drifts toward Additive Manufacturing or Smart Materials and Structures. Right now the framing still supports JMD, especially because the manuscript emphasizes parameterization, search strategy, and design tradeoffs, but the final Discussion will need to connect the results back to design methodology rather than only to test outcomes.

Minor comments

1. The manuscript still has placeholder/synthetic BO figures (LOOCV, sensitivity, convergence, Pareto). That is acceptable for internal drafting but not for submission. The captions are honest about this.

2. The “high-fidelity validation experiments using pretensioned tensegrity assemblies” contribution is not yet fully reconciled with the later “metal-analog validation” wording. It appears the intent is true-cable metal analogs with measured pretension, but the paper should state that directly and consistently.

3. The quasi-static standards paragraph cites several ASTM/ISO documents adapted to architected polymer cells. That is fine, but the final paper should separate what was actually followed from what was consulted.

4. The print-parameter table is still largely TBD. That is a hard gate for publication.

5. The out-of-scope statement is appropriate and should remain: off-axis/combined loading, multi-hit/cyclic durability, and landing-attitude variability are future work.

Editorial comments

1. Remove the Introduction TODO about clarifying the gap versus Pajunen and Mo by actually writing those sentences.
2. Remove all manuscript-status TODO text before submission.
3. Replace “to our knowledge” formulations with explicit scope-bounded claims where possible.
4. The novelty table is useful; consider renaming it from generic “Positioning of this work” to something closer to “Scope-relative novelty positioning.”
5. Make sure “Table 1” references are consistent with JMD production style after final typesetting.

Bottom line

This round is closer to publishable form than round 4. The literature-positioning problem is now largely fixed. The remaining barriers are not the high-level framing anymore; they are the lack of real results, incomplete process/test disclosure, and the need to show that the chosen BO machinery is not just fashionable but necessary and empirically supported for this search space.


Mock Reviewer #2 -- Biomechanics / Impact Mechanics

Recommendation: Major Revision

The manuscript is more disciplined than prior rounds about what it does and does not claim. I appreciate that the authors now state plainly that the present study is limited to single-cell, fixed-topology T3-prism specimens under axial quasi-static and drop-weight loading, and that off-axis loading, combined loading, multi-hit/cyclic durability, and landing-attitude variability are future work. That honesty helps.

My main concern is that the application motivation and the test configuration are still not fully aligned.

Major comments

1. The motivation is split between planetary landing and later crutch-tip translation, but the mechanical evidence chain is still thin.
The manuscript front end references planetary-landing tensegrity systems and “aerospace landing structures,” while the Discussion contains a future-work path toward crutch-tip miniaturization. That ordering is good in the sense that the crutch-tip concept is no longer driving the Introduction. Still, for a biomechanics/impact reader, the paper must decide what primary use-case the current axial test actually informs.

If the main motivation is planetary/payload landing, then the paper should explain more explicitly how the axial drop-tower observables map to that use-case. If the main motivation is eventual assistive-device cushioning, then the present fixture is even further removed from the real loading envelope. The current text sits in between.

2. The axial fixture is acceptable as a first screening test, but the manuscript should not imply more transferability than it has earned.
The paper now does a decent job limiting scope, but the drop protocol still uses a constrained specimen in a bungee-assisted drop tower where unconstrained specimens would otherwise lift off the base. That is a very specific apparatus-dependent loading scenario. It may still be useful for comparing candidate geometries under controlled axial events, but it is not a surrogate for realistic off-axis touchdown, repeated contacts, or user-device interactions.

I would want the final paper to say more explicitly that the current impact rig is a comparative screening platform, not a faithful recreation of the operational loading environment.

3. The metric mapping remains a critical issue: SEA is not the same thing as injury-relevant cushioning.
The revised BO formulation improves this by making peak transmitted force a hard constraint and optimizing SEA and compaction efficiency only within that admissible region. That is the right direction. It addresses one of the big issues from earlier rounds: high SEA alone can reward absorbers that still transmit unacceptable peaks.

Even so, the manuscript should explain in plain mechanics terms why the rigid-control-derived threshold F* is the right admissibility boundary. Is it a relative-improvement threshold only, or is it intended to approximate a use-case-based force ceiling? Right now it appears to be a control-relative threshold, which is methodologically okay for screening, but weaker as an application-specific claim.

4. The planned shock-processing language is better, but still needs real data and full protocol disclosure.
The manuscript properly cites SAE J211 for CFC-180 filtering and shows a synthetic mechanistic figure with impulse-consistent traces. Good conceptually. But until the actual sampling rate, sensor mounting, channel conditioning, drop heights, and event-window definitions are reported, the impact conclusions remain provisional.

5. The metal-analog transfer test is interesting but should be framed as exploratory, exactly as the current text says.
This is one of the stronger revised sections. The paper explicitly notes that deformation modes, joint compliance, friction, pretension behavior, and strain-rate sensitivity differ between PLA/TPU and Al/SS systems, and therefore agreement is not expected a priori. Good. Keep that language. The pre-specified Spearman rank-correlation criterion is also a sensible way to keep the claim ordinal rather than over-quantitative.

Minor comments

1. The planned Lansmont M23 replicate campaign for selected Pareto designs is a good addition. If completed, it could strengthen the dynamic-mechanics side substantially.

2. The manuscript should distinguish more clearly between what is measured directly in quasi-static compression and what is inferred or adapted for dynamic interpretation.

3. The phrase “out-cushion the uncushioned baseline” is intuitive but a bit informal for the final paper.

4. If the final paper keeps a planetary-landing motivation, consider adding one short paragraph linking the chosen metrics to the usual landing-system concerns: peak deceleration, impulse redistribution, stroke/compaction, and mass efficiency.

Bottom line

The manuscript has improved because the optimization target is now better matched to impact relevance than in earlier drafts. Still, the current study is a controlled axial screening framework, not yet a convincing application-level validation for either planetary landing or assistive-device biomechanics. That is fine, but the paper should say exactly that.


Mock Reviewer #3 -- Additive Manufacturing / Materials

Recommendation: Major Revision

The paper is more credible on the additive-manufacturing side than in prior rounds. The authors now use the newly integrated tensegrity-AM literature appropriately: not as proof of their exact junction/process concept, but as evidence that printed tensegrity-inspired architectures can be made and can show useful mechanical behavior. That is the right rhetorical move. I no longer see the major literature-positioning omission that was still open previously.

My remaining concerns are about processing evidence and manufacturability disclosure, not literature awareness.

Major comments

1. The PLA+TPU multi-material processing claims are plausible, but still under-documented.
The manuscript states that specimens are printed on a Bambu Lab H2D with PLA struts and TPU tendons in a single build, and that the support strategy uses a lowered support threshold plus manually generated narrowing pillars for near-vertical TPU members. That is useful. The Supplementary Information also helps by documenting the support-generation workflow and selected joint concept.

But Table 3 (print parameters) is still mostly TBD: nozzle temperatures, bed temperature, layer height, print speed, infill. For AM reviewers, these are not optional details. Without them, the repeatability and interface quality claims cannot be evaluated.

2. The internal-anchor joint is interesting, but at present it is a design hypothesis more than a validated contribution.
The core claim is that locating the TPU-PLA interface inside a rigid strut-end cage may improve durability relative to exposed overmold-like interfaces. That is mechanically plausible. The manuscript is also careful to say Ye et al. is only a precedent for co-printing, not validation of the present junction. Good.

However, the contribution statement still says this joint geometry is intended to improve cyclic interface durability, while multiple TODOs note that pull-out and fatigue verification remains outstanding. Until those tests are done, the paper should phrase the joint contribution as a proposed manufacturable junction architecture, not as a demonstrated durability advance.

3. The manuscript does a good job acknowledging resolution limits, but the consequences should be pushed further.
The as-built-resolution paragraph is one of the better revisions in this round. It admits that d_s and d_t are only nominally continuous and that realized diameters are quantized by nozzle/line-width/support interactions. Good. That honesty matters.

What is still needed is a clearer statement of how large the as-built spread is relative to the BO step size. If the dimensional noise is a substantial fraction of the search-space granularity, then the effective optimization problem is partly process optimization, not just geometry optimization.

4. FDM repeatability and interfacial reliability remain open gates.
The Results section has a placeholder for reproducibility across print replicates, which is exactly the right thing to report. Until those data exist, the paper cannot support strong claims about BO convergence on a noisy manufacturing platform. Likewise, interface strength characterization is still pending. Those are major gates.

5. The metal-analog plan is conceptually useful, but it does not validate the polymer printing process.
The Al/SS study may validate rank transfer of the geometry concept. It does not substitute for polymer-process validation. The manuscript mostly respects that distinction, but I would keep it explicit.

6. The newly integrated tensegrity-AM references are used reasonably well, but the manuscript should avoid flattening important differences among them.
Bauer, Pajunen 2021, and Sabouni-Zawadzka establish additive manufacturability and tunable/static behavior in tensegrity-inspired systems. Almeida and Davami are closer to dynamic loading relevance. Wang 2026 is closest in spirit to integrated rigid-flexible fabrication/validation. The manuscript mostly handles this correctly. I would just ask the authors not to compress these papers into a generic “therefore our process is established” statement. They establish the architecture class, not the specific PLA/TPU H2D process window or the internal-anchor joint.

Minor comments

1. The support strategy for near-vertical TPU tendons is important enough that one concise quantitative success criterion in the main paper would help.

2. If feasible, report actual measured tendon/strut diameters from a pilot batch, even before the full BO campaign, because that would ground the “realized geometry” discussion.

3. The statement that all specimens are printed vertically and arranged 3x3 on one plate is useful. Consider also reporting whether part location on the plate is randomized or balanced across BO batches to avoid spatial process bias.

4. The selected dovetail joint with anchor-bulb backup is described in the SI. That is fine, but one small schematic of the selected joint in the main text could help readers who never open the SI.

Bottom line

The AM framing is much better and the literature gap is closed. The paper is still gated by incomplete process disclosure and absent validation data on repeatability and interface durability. With those added, the paper could become solid. Without them, the manufacturing claims remain partly aspirational.


Mock Editor (JMD Associate Editor) decision letter

Decision: Major Revision

This fifth-round revision is a meaningful improvement over the round-4 submission. In particular, the specific round-4 request to integrate the relevant tensegrity/additive-manufacturing literature has now been addressed. The manuscript appropriately incorporates Bauer et al. (2021), Pajunen et al. (2021), Sabouni-Zawadzka et al. (2024), Almeida et al. (2025), Davami et al. (2025), and Wang et al. (2026), and uses them in a measured way to position the present study relative to prior work on printed tensegrity-inspired architectures. On that point, the prior reference deficiency appears resolved. The paper is also better structured than in the previous round: the constrained multi-objective Bayesian-optimization formulation is clearer, the active design variables and fixed-joint rationale are more consistent, and the out-of-scope boundaries are now stated directly. That said, the manuscript remains at a planned-methods stage, with placeholder Results and Discussion, synthetic illustrative BO/impact figures, incomplete process/test parameter disclosure, and unresolved validation of key manufacturing claims. For those reasons, I cannot move the paper beyond Major Revision at this time.

With respect to venue fit, the manuscript remains potentially suitable for ASME Journal of Mechanical Design provided the final revision keeps the center of gravity on design representation, design-space parameterization, experiment-driven optimization, and design-tradeoff discovery. In its current state, it is still close enough to JMD because the framing emphasizes the design methodology rather than only materials processing or impact characterization. However, if the eventual completed paper leans primarily on fabrication process development or impact-test phenomenology, it may fit more naturally in Additive Manufacturing or Smart Materials and Structures. The present revision moves the manuscript closer to acceptance relative to the round-4 Major Revision decision, but not yet to the point of a minor-revision path.

Required revisions before resubmission, in priority order

1. Replace all placeholder Results and Discussion content with real experimental results and interpretation.
This is the main gate. The current Results section is entirely placeholder text, and the Discussion remains a topic list. A JMD research paper cannot be evaluated for acceptance without actual findings.

2. Replace all synthetic illustrative figures with figures generated from the reported campaign data.
This includes the BO diagnostics/convergence/Pareto figures and the impact-response figures now labeled as synthetic examples.

3. Complete the fabrication and test-method disclosures.
The print-parameter table still contains multiple TBD fields, and the testing section still lacks the exact fixtures, load-cell ranges, sampling rate, DAQ details, drop heights, and replicate-handling protocol. These are required for reproducibility.

4. Tighten and narrow the novelty claim in the Introduction and Discussion.
The revised literature review now supports a scoped claim. The authors should state explicitly, in plain text, that the contribution is the combination of a multi-material PLA/TPU tensegrity-inspired architecture, the selected printable internal-anchor joint concept, and an experiment-driven BO loop trained directly on physical measurements. Avoid broader “first” claims about printed tensegrity absorbers or dynamic tensegrity response.

5. Empirically justify the BO choices on the actual campaign data.
The manuscript should report the promised benchmark of SAASBO versus a standard single-task GP baseline for this approximately five-variable continuous search space, and should discuss whether the inferred homoscedastic noise model was adequate. The constrained multi-objective formulation itself is well motivated and should be retained.

6. Clarify the handling of commanded versus realized geometry.
The current text correctly notes that member diameters are only nominally continuous and that as-built dimensions should be measured. The revision should show exactly how realized geometry is recorded and used in the surrogate model.

7. Reconcile the validation language.
The contribution statement refers to “pretensioned” tensegrity validation with true cables and measured pretension, whereas the later section describes a metal-analog Al/SS rank-transfer study. If these are the same validation activity, say so directly and consistently.

8. Moderate and verify the manufacturing claims about the internal-anchor joint.
Until pull-out/fatigue evidence is presented, the junction should be framed as a proposed manufacturable design intended to improve durability, not as a demonstrated durability improvement.

9. Keep the application framing aligned with the actual evidence.
The current axial drop protocol is best presented as a controlled screening framework. The revision should avoid overstating transfer to realistic off-axis, repeated-contact, or field-use scenarios.

10. Remove all remaining manuscript-status and drafting TODO material.
This includes the visible planned-methods note, unresolved gap-note text, and other internal drafting comments.

Editorial assessment of prior asks

- Round-3 bibliographic/method issues: previously identified gaps regarding SAASBO, TuRBO, SEA/densification metrics, and SAE J211 appear closed in the present draft.
- Round-4 bibliographic issue: the request to integrate the tensegrity-additive-manufacturing literature is now resolved.
- Remaining barrier: not literature coverage, but absence of completed evidence.


Reviewers' bibliographic gaps

The major bibliographic gaps from prior rounds are now closed: SAASBO, TuRBO, SEA/densification metrics, SAE J211, and the round-4 tensegrity-AM reference set are all now represented.

Possible remaining additions, if the authors want to strengthen specific points further, are modest rather than mandatory:

- Tensegrity parameterization / heterogeneous-member design
  - If the manuscript keeps discussing future relaxation from D3-symmetric shared diameters to per-orbit or per-member parameterization, it would help to add one peer-reviewed source on heterogeneous tensegrity parameterization or optimization rather than relying on an internal TODO note.

- Architected-material BO with physical experiments
  - The current BO citations are adequate for methods. If the final Results emphasize experimental, not simulation, closed-loop materials discovery, one or two additional peer-reviewed examples of BO run directly on physical experiments in materials/mechanical systems could strengthen external validity. This is optional, not a clear gap.

- FDM multimaterial interface durability / cyclic performance
  - If the authors continue to discuss durability motivation for the internal-anchor junction, they may want one or two stronger peer-reviewed references specifically on cyclic durability or fatigue of rigid-soft FDM interfaces, beyond interface/printing-parameter studies alone.

- Impact mechanics / cushioning metric interpretation
  - If the final paper makes stronger application claims from axial impact metrics, one additional peer-reviewed citation explicitly linking transmitted-force/impulse/stroke metrics to absorber design criteria in impact mitigation would help. The current SEA/densification citations are acceptable, so this is a strengthening suggestion, not a missing-core-reference issue.

- AM tensegrity comparison table
  - Not a missing citation requirement, but the authors may consider whether one or two of the newly integrated AM tensegrity papers closest to their scope (likely Almeida 2025, Davami 2025, or Wang 2026) should appear directly in the comparison/novelty table rather than only in prose.

- Discretionary analytical decisions made during the analysis
  - Focused the review on manuscript structure, framing, methods rigor, literature integration, internal consistency, and venue fit, rather than numerical performance, because the manuscript explicitly remains at the planned-methods stage.
  - Treated clean-source text in manuscript-body.tex and supplementary.tex as the primary evidence source, using README.md and references.bib as supporting documents.
  - Interpreted the recommendation threshold conservatively: because Results/Discussion remain placeholders and several methods tables/figures are incomplete, assigned Major Revision rather than Minor Revision despite improvement in literature coverage.
  - Evaluated novelty claims against the narrowest defensible formulation supported by the cited literature: multi-material PLA/TPU FDM plus internal-anchor joint plus experiment-driven BO on physical data.
  - Assessed JMD venue fit based on current manuscript emphasis on design parameterization and optimization methodology, while noting potential drift toward Additive Manufacturing or Smart Materials and Structures depending on how final results are written.
  - Treated the metal-analog Al/SS study as an exploratory rank-transfer validation, consistent with the manuscript’s pre-specified Spearman rho_s criterion, rather than as a direct material equivalence validation.
  - Considered unresolved TODOs that the user explicitly marked as intentionally open as gating context for final recommendation, but did not reframe them as “new defects” where the manuscript already flags them honestly.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

\todo[inline,color=blue!20]{\textbf{Manuscript status.} At time of
writing the project is at the \emph{planned-methods} phase: the
parameterized unit cell, multi-material print recipe, joint geometry,

campaign has not yet produced reportable results. Sections~\ref{sec:results}
and~\ref{sec:discussion} therefore remain placeholders.}

Tensegrity structures are assemblies of rigid compression members
suspended within a continuous network of tension members; their defining
property, that no two rigid bars touch, yields lightweight assemblies with
remarkable strength-to-weight ratios and tunable nonlinear mechanical
responses~\citep{skelton2009tensegrity, sultan2009tensegrity}. These
properties have made tensegrity attractive across scales, from
metamaterial unit cells~\citep{amendola2014experimental,
zhang2018tensegrity, fraternali2015tensegrity} to compliant impact-absorbing
robots developed for planetary landing~\citep{agogino2018superball,
caluwaerts2014superball, sabelhaus2015system, vespignani2018design,
deitrich2022titan}. Recent work has shown that \emph{tensegrity-inspired}
unit cells can be directly 3D-printed and exhibit load-limiting plateaus
under drop-weight impact~\citep{pajunen2019design}, opening a path
toward additively manufactured architected absorbers. Throughout, we use
\emph{tensegrity-inspired} to denote printable unit cells that adopt the
characteristic tensegrity motif---rigid compression members carried by a
network of pretensioned soft tension elements---while relaxing the strict
classical requirement that no two compression members touch and that the
tension members behave as ideal inextensible cables; here the tension elements
are extruded TPU and the struts may share printed junctions.

Multi-material fused-deposition modeling (FDM) that pairs a rigid polymer
such as polylactic acid (PLA) with a soft, rate-dependent elastomer such as
thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) has been used to fabricate rigid--soft
architected energy absorbers on a single platform---for example, thick-panel
origami metamaterials with PLA panels and TPU hinges~\citep{ye2023multimaterial}
and ABS/TPU honeycombs with tunable stiff/flexible
proportions~\citep{khatri2024energy}. The same rigid--soft co-printing
capability makes it possible to rapidly fabricate diverse tensegrity-inspired
geometries, which adopt a discrete-compression/continuous-tension topology
rather than an origami or honeycomb one. Although extruded TPU does not behave
as an idealized
inextensible cable, its rate-dependent damping is a desirable property
for impact-absorption applications and complements the elastic stiffness
of the PLA compression members rather than competing with it.

Designing such architected absorbers is fundamentally a
\emph{design-of-experiments} problem: the configuration space spanned by
strut geometry, tension-element cross-section, connectivity, and
unit-cell tiling is large; each candidate must be physically printed
and tested; and the relevant performance metrics---peak transmitted
force, specific energy absorption (SEA), and compaction
efficiency---are noisy and partially correlated. Bayesian optimization
(BO) is well-matched to this regime, having driven breakthroughs from
hyperparameter tuning of AlphaGo~\citep{silver2016mastering} to
sustainable concrete~\citep{ament2023sustainable}, autonomous
discovery of organic laser emitters~\citep{striethkalthoff2024delocalized},
and architected materials~\citep{mo2023accelerated, wang2022bayesian,
lee2023bayesian, zhang2021bo}.

    operates directly on
    physical quasi-static compression and drop-weight impact
    measurements, recommending the next designs to

\subsection{Multi-Material 3D Printing of PLA/TPU Composites}

Multi-material rigid--soft FDM enables stiff/compliant combinations on a
single platform with tunable energy absorption, demonstrated for thick-panel
origami with PLA (or ABS/CFRP) panels and TPU hinges~\cite{ye2023multimaterial}
and for ABS--TPU honeycombs~\cite{khatri2024energy}. Neither study is itself a
tensegrity, but both establish the rigid--soft co-printing route we adopt. Ye
et~al.~\cite{ye2023multimaterial}
introduced a \emph{wrapping-based} strategy in which rigid cores are
encapsulated by continuous soft skins, reported to reduce interface
delamination under cyclic loading, something we take inspiration from in our
designs.
Beyond these rigid--soft demonstrations, a growing body of work confirms
that genuinely tensegrity-inspired architectures can be additively
manufactured and exhibit programmable mechanical response. Bauer
et~al.~\cite{bauer2021tensegrity} showed that 3D-printed tensegrity
metamaterials delocalize deformation to resist catastrophic failure, while
Pajunen et~al.~\cite{pajunen2021prestrain} tuned acoustic bandgaps in
3D-printed tensegrity-inspired lattices through prestrain, and
Sabouni-Zawadzka et~al.~\cite{sabounizawadzka2024experimental}
experimentally characterized 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired metamaterials
built on the simplex module. More directly relevant to impact, Almeida
et~al.~\cite{almeida2025highstrainrate} and Davami
et~al.~\cite{davami2025dynamicanalysis} characterized the high-strain-rate
and dynamic response of additively manufactured tensegrity-inspired
structures, and Wang et~al.~\cite{wang2026integrated} reported an
integrated fabrication-and-validation workflow for tensegrity-inspired
rigid--flexible metamaterials. Collectively these studies establish the
additive-manufacturability, tunability, and impact relevance of the
architecture class adopted here, none combining multi-material FDM with an
experiment-driven optimization loop.

composites~\citep{arifvianto2022mechanicalpropertiesof,
ruwais2025mechanicalperformanceof} report quantitative bounds on
stiffness, strength, and energy absorption for the same PLA--TPU pair
used here, while FDM PLA fatigue
data~\citep{ezeh2018onthefatigue, vanaei2021multiscaledamageanalysis}
inform conservative design bounds for the rigid struts.
Architected multi-material lattices with co-printed compliant skins
have been explicitly designed for high specific energy
absorption~\citep{yavas2022designandfabrication}, with FDM-specific
multimaterial interface adhesion (notably TPU bonded to rigid
co-printed substrates) characterized
in~\citep{caminero2019printingparameters}; recent surveys catalogue the
rapidly expanding additively manufactured polymeric energy-absorption
literature~\citep{bustihan2026recentadvancesin,

\subsection{Bayesian Optimization for Architected-Material Design}

Bayesian optimization is a sequential, model-based strategy for
optimizing expensive black-box functions using a Gaussian-process
surrogate~\citep{shahriari2016taking, frazier2018tutorial}. Modern
implementations such as BoTorch~\citep{balandat2020botorch} and the Ax
platform built atop it~\citep{pmlr-v293-olson25a} support
parallel batched evaluations and a wide variety of acquisition
functions; recent algorithmic advances include log-EI for numerical
robustness~\citep{ament2023logei}, noisy expected hypervolume
improvement for multi-objective settings~\citep{daulton2021nehvi},
input-noise-robust acquisitions~\citep{daulton2022robust}, and
evolution-guided constrained multi-objective BO for self-driving
labs~\citep{low2024evolution}. Mixed/categorical search spaces---needed
for the planned connectivity-topology extension rather than the
continuous $T_3$-prism prototype studied here---have dedicated
treatments in BOCS~\citep{baptista2018bocs} and the
one-hot-with-rounded-kernel construction
of~\citep{garridomerchan2020dealingwithcategorical}. BO has been
applied to mechanical metamaterial and structural
design~\citep{wang2022bayesian, lee2023bayesian, mo2023accelerated}
and to additive manufacturing~\citep{zhang2021bo}.
Mo et~al.~\cite{mo2023accelerated} in
particular established a multifidelity BO framework for architected
materials by fusing low-fidelity simulations with high-fidelity
ground truth via nonlinear information-fusion
priors~\citep{perdikaris2017nonlinear}; the present work shifts the
emphasis from simulation surrogates to direct experimental data,
appropriate for materials whose constitutive response is difficult to
calibrate from first principles.

Experiment-Driven Bayesian Optimization Loop}
\label{sec:methods:bo}

The optimization loop maintains a Gaussian-process (GP) surrogate over
the design space defined in
Section~\ref{sec:methods:parameterization}. After each round of physical
experiments, the GP is updated and an acquisition function is maximized
to recommend the next batch of designs to fabricate. The primary
reported campaign is posed as a \emph{constrained multi-objective}
problem: simultaneously maximize specific energy absorption (SEA) and
compaction efficiency $\eta_c$ subject to an upper bound on peak
transmitted force $F_{\max} \le F^{\star}$, where $F^{\star}$ is fixed
from the rigid-control drop response so that admissible designs must
out-cushion the uncushioned baseline. Implementation
uses BoTorch~\citep{balandat2020botorch} with noisy Expected
Hypervolume Improvement
(qNEHVI)~\citep{daulton2021nehvi} as the acquisition function; the
hypervolume reference point is anchored at the rigid-control
$(\mathrm{SEA},\eta_c)$ pair so that improvement is measured against the
no-absorber baseline. A single-objective
log-Expected-Improvement (LogEI) run~\citep{ament2023logei} on SEA
(with the same force constraint) is retained only as a baseline for
quantifying the benefit of the multi-objective formulation. The
input-noise-robust acquisition of Daulton
et~al.~\cite{daulton2022robust} and the evolution-guided constrained
variant of Low et~al.~\cite{low2024evolution} are held in reserve as a
contingency, to be adopted only if between-print variability is found
to dominate the objective signal; they are not part of the default
reported loop.
The working $T_3$-prism search space is fully continuous (the five
variables of Table~\ref{tab:design-vars}), so no categorical encoding
is required for the present campaign; the mixed-search-space
constructions of~\citep{garridomerchan2020dealingwithcategorical} and
the BOCS combinatorial baseline~\citep{baptista2018bocs} are noted as
the route for the future connectivity-topology categorical
(Section~\ref{sec:methods:parameterization}) rather than as part of
the current loop.

The GP surrogate uses a Mat\'ern-5/2 kernel with automatic relevance
determination (ARD), i.e.\ a separate length scale per input dimension,
so that per-variable sensitivities can be read directly from the fitted
length scales. Inputs are normalized to the unit cube and outputs are
standardized; observation noise is \emph{inferred} by the model (a
learned homoscedastic noise level) rather than fixed a priori. The
campaign budget is an $n = 9$ Sobol initialization batch
(Table~\ref{tab:design-vars}) followed by $T = 10$ sequential
optimization batches of $q = 5$ prints each, i.e.\ $9 + 50 = 59$
specimens in total. Random seeds for the Sobol generator and
the acquisition optimizer are recorded per batch so that each
recommendation is reproducible.\todo{Confirm the final budget
($T=10$ batches of $q=5$) against printer throughput once the campaign
is underway.}

\paragraph{Implementation status.} The campaign harness is built on
the Ax platform~\citep{pmlr-v293-olson25a}. The working $T_3$-prism
search space is the five-variable continuous box of
Table~\ref{tab:design-vars}; Ax's \texttt{HierarchicalSearchSpace}
machinery is reserved for the planned topology/tiling extensions
(Section~\ref{sec:methods:parameterization}) and is not exercised by
the current continuous-only prototype. The first physical batch
consists of $n = 9$ specimens generated by a Sobol sequence over these
five variables and printed in a single $3 \times 3$ plate layout.
For this ${\sim}5$--$6$-variable space the default acquisition pairing
is sparse axis-aligned subspace BO (SAASBO)~\citep{eriksson2021saasbo}
with qNEHVI. We retain
SAASBO even though the dimensionality is modest because its strong

\subsection{Multi-Material 3D Printing of PLA/TPU Composites}

Multi-material rigid--soft FDM enables stiff/compliant combinations on a
single platform with tunable energy absorption, demonstrated for thick-panel
origami with PLA (or ABS/CFRP) panels and TPU hinges~\cite{ye2023multimaterial}
and for ABS--TPU honeycombs~\cite{khatri2024energy}. Neither study is itself a
tensegrity, but both establish the rigid--soft co-printing route we adopt. Ye
et~al.~\cite{ye2023multimaterial}
introduced a \emph{wrapping-based} strategy in which rigid cores are
encapsulated by continuous soft skins, reported to reduce interface
delamination under cyclic loading, something we take inspiration from in our
designs.
Beyond these rigid--soft demonstrations, a growing body of work confirms
that genuinely tensegrity-inspired architectures can be additively
manufactured and exhibit programmable mechanical response. Bauer
et~al.~\cite{bauer2021tensegrity} showed that 3D-printed tensegrity
metamaterials delocalize deformation to resist catastrophic failure, while
Pajunen et~al.~\cite{pajunen2021prestrain} tuned acoustic bandgaps in
3D-printed tensegrity-inspired lattices through prestrain, and
Sabouni-Zawadzka et~al.~\cite{sabounizawadzka2024experimental}
experimentally characterized 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired metamaterials
built on the simplex module. More directly relevant to impact, Almeida
et~al.~\cite{almeida2025highstrainrate} and Davami
et~al.~\cite{davami2025dynamicanalysis} characterized the high-strain-rate
and dynamic response of additively manufactured tensegrity-inspired
structures, and Wang et~al.~\cite{wang2026integrated} reported an
integrated fabrication-and-validation workflow for tensegrity-inspired
rigid--flexible metamaterials. Collectively these studies establish the
additive-manufacturability, tunability, and impact relevance of the
architecture class adopted here, none combining multi-material FDM with an
experiment-driven optimization loop.
Recent multi-material PLA/TPU sandwich and layered
composites~\citep{arifvianto2022mechanicalpropertiesof,
ruwais2025mechanicalperformanceof} report quantitative bounds on
stiffness, strength, and energy absorption for the same PLA--TPU pair
used here, while FDM PLA fatigue
data~\citep{ezeh2018onthefatigue, vanaei2021multiscaledamageanalysis}
inform conservative design bounds for the rigid struts.
Architected multi-material lattices with co-printed compliant skins
have been explicitly designed for high specific energy
absorption~\citep{yavas2022designandfabrication}, with FDM-specific
multimaterial interface adhesion (notably TPU bonded to rigid
co-printed substrates) characterized
in~\citep{caminero2019printingparameters}; recent surveys catalogue the
rapidly expanding additively manufactured polymeric energy-absorption
literature~\citep{bustihan2026recentadvancesin,
liu2026threedimensionalprintedlattice}. \todo{Add a short paragraph on
relevant TPU/PETG tensegrity search-space bounds once the Edison
literature task \texttt{5ae24eaf-5b6e-45cf-9f6c-1c7fbd881738}
synthesis is integrated.}

\subsection{Bayesian Optimization for Architected-Material Design}

Bayesian optimization is a sequential, model-based strategy for
optimizing expensive black-box functions using a Gaussian-process
surrogate~\citep{shahriari2016taking, frazier2018tutorial}. Modern
implementations such as BoTorch~\citep{balandat2020botorch} and the Ax
platform built atop it~\citep{pmlr-v293-olson25a} support
parallel batched evaluations and a wide variety of acquisition
functions; recent algorithmic advances include log-EI for numerical
robustness~\citep{ament2023logei}, noisy expected hypervolume
improvement for multi-objective settings~\citep{daulton2021nehvi},
input-noise-robust acquisitions~\citep{daulton2022robust}, and
evolution-guided constrained multi-objective BO for self-driving
labs~\citep{low2024evolution}. Mixed/categorical search spaces---needed
for the planned connectivity-topology extension rather than the
continuous $T_3$-prism prototype studied here---have dedicated
treatments in BOCS~\citep{baptista2018bocs} and the
one-hot-with-rounded-kernel construction
of~\citep{garridomerchan2020dealingwithcategorical}. BO has been
applied to mechanical metamaterial and structural
design~\citep{wang2022bayesian, lee2023bayesian, mo2023accelerated}
and to additive manufacturing~\citep{zhang2021bo}.
Mo et~al.~\cite{mo2023accelerated} in
particular established a multifidelity BO framework for architected
materials by fusing low-fidelity simulations with high-fidelity
ground truth via nonlinear information-fusion
priors~\citep{perdikaris2017nonlinear}; the present work shifts the
emphasis from simulation surrogates to direct experimental data,
appropriate for materials whose constitutive response is difficult to
calibrate from first principles.

Multi-Material Fabrication}
\label{sec:methods:fabrication}

Specimens are fabricated on a multi-material FDM printer using PLA for
the rigid struts and TPU for the soft tension elements.
Figure~\ref{fig:fab-workflow} summarizes the end-to-end fabrication and
characterization workflow, from parametric CAD through multi-material
slicing, dual-extrusion printing, post-processing, and mechanical
testing. Rather than
wrapping the struts in a continuous TPU skin, the current design anchors
the TPU tension elements \emph{inside} the ends of each PLA strut: the
cables converging at a given strut end are joined within the strut,
which acts as a rigid cage housing the junction, and the individual
tendons then exit through discrete outlets. This keeps the soft--rigid
interface in internal, compression-dominated pockets rather than at an
exposed overmolded surface. This construction effectively inverts the
material roles of Ye et~al.'s soft-skin-over-rigid-core
wrapping~\cite{ye2023multimaterial}: here a soft TPU core is captured within
a rigid PLA shell, so we cite that work only as a multi-material co-printing
precedent rather than as validation of the present junction. \todo{Quantitatively
verify the internal-anchoring junction strength against the PR~\#39 / PR~\#35
joint pull-out studies before making any cyclic-durability claim.} \todo{Document slicer profile
(layer height, infill, print speed, nozzle temperatures, retraction
settings) and validation prints used to characterize PLA--TPU interface
strength.}

\paragraph{Print platform and joint geometry.} The working platform is
a Bambu Lab~H2D printer, which permits a single rigid--soft build
without filament swaps. Strut endpoints are tied to cables through
parametric joint geometries developed and ranked through a five-design
OpenSCAD study (anchor-bulb, dovetail, TPU-sleeve overmold,
eyelet-loop, and TPU-rebar variants); the working prototype uses a
dovetail joint (Design~B) with an anchor-bulb backup (Design~A) for
sensitivity studies, with a captive TPU core routed inside the PLA
shell to keep the soft tendon protected from layer-line failure at
the strut-to-cable transition. The full five-design comparison and the
selected junction are detailed in the Supplementary Information.\todo{Cite the
joint-design Phase-3 CAD review (Edison ANALYSIS \texttt{19e0c868}) and the
Phase-4 vision review (\texttt{e9a1f4cc}) once both are integrated into the
references.}

\paragraph{Supports for soft members.} Because near-vertical TPU
tendons are otherwise unsupported during printing, the slicer profile
combines a tensegrity-specific Bambu Studio recipe (support threshold
angle dropped from~40\textdegree{} to~10\textdegree, support material
matched to the rigid extruder) with manually generated narrowing
pillars that ray-cast against the printable mesh underside, producing
TPU-safe coverage of vertical members without slicer-side painting.
Full workflow details are provided in the Supplementary Information.

Experimental Characterization}
\label{sec:methods:testing}

Each printed specimen is subjected to two physical tests:

\paragraph{Quasi-static compression.} A uniaxial load--displacement
curve is recorded on a benchtop electromechanical load frame
(BYU CB~123 Instron) following best-practice combinations of
ASTM~D638, ASTM~D412, ASTM~E111, ASTM~F2971, and
ISO/ASTM~52900/52921 adapted to architected polymer cells. Because
expected cell stiffnesses fall in the $\sim$5--30\,g force range, the
default 5\,kN load cell is over-ranged and is being replaced by a
100--500\,N cell for the first campaign.\todo{Cite the Instron-stiffness
Edison LITERATURE\_HIGH brief (\texttt{9f68e71e}) once the entry is
added to \texttt{references.bib}.} Reported metrics are
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{SEA} \;=\; \frac{1}{m}\!\int_{0}^{\delta_d}\! F(\delta)\,
  \mathrm{d}\delta,
  \qquad
  \eta_c \;=\; \frac{\int_{0}^{\delta_d}\! F(\delta)\,\mathrm{d}\delta}{F_{\max}\,\delta_d},
\end{equation}
where $m$ is the specimen mass, $\delta_d$ is the densification
displacement, $F_{\max}$ is the peak transmitted force, and $\eta_c$ is
the compaction efficiency. To keep these metrics objective and
reproducible, the densification displacement $\delta_d$ is taken as the
displacement at which the energy-absorption efficiency--displacement curve
reaches its maximum ($\mathrm{d}\eta/\mathrm{d}\delta = 0$), and $F_{\max}$
is the maximum force recorded \emph{within} the integration window
$[0,\delta_d]$ rather than a global or post-densification peak. These
energy-absorption-diagram definitions of densification displacement and
compaction (energy-absorption) efficiency follow the canonical cellular-solid
treatments of Gibson and Ashby~\citep{gibson1997cellular}, Avalle
et~al.~\citep{avalle2001characterization}, Tan
et~al.~\citep{tan2005dynamic}, and Michailidis
et~al.~\citep{michailidis2011establishment}.

\paragraph{Drop-weight impact.} Following Pajunen
et~al.~\cite{pajunen2019design},
specimens are subjected to drop-weight impact tests with instrumented
load cells; we report the peak transmitted force and the energy-absorption
plateau characteristics. Figure~\ref{fig:dropcurve} illustrates the
mechanism-oriented presentation we adopt for these processed deceleration
traces, linking features of the measured signal to the structural events that
produce them. The primary fixture is a bungee-assisted
laboratory drop tower in which the base accelerates downward faster
than~$1g$; because unconstrained specimens lift off the base during
descent by design of the rig, the protocol constrains the specimen
top through light tethers (capping upward travel) and registers the
base via transfer tape or V-block features so that loading-direction
compliance is not altered.\todo{Cite the drop-test protocol document
(PR~\#67) and the drop-test Edison LITERATURE\_HIGH brief
(\texttt{653d7d39}) once integrated.} A higher-fidelity replicate
campaign on a Lansmont~M23 shock/cushion tester (per ASTM~D1596) with
synchronized Polytec~QTec
laser vibrometry is planned for selected Pareto-optimal designs.\todo{%
Cite the M23~+~QTec equipment brief (Edison LITERATURE\_HIGH
\texttt{1a0f4a70}) once integrated.} Slip resistance and traction at
the specimen--floor interface---governed by the tip geometry rather
than the internal lattice---follow the test methodology of ISO
11334-4~\citep{iso11334-4} for walking-aid tips and are out of scope
for the present axial-impact study.

Metal-Analog Validation}
\label{sec:methods:validation}

To test whether the rankings learned on the printed PLA/TPU specimens
generalize beyond the as-printed polymer system, a final validation
campaign reproduces a subset of the $T_3$-prism designs as
\emph{metal analogs} built from hollow aluminum rods (compression
members) and stainless-steel threaded cables (tension members), using
the same $R$, $H$, $\theta$, and member-diameter parameterization.
Rather than fabricating only the top-ranked geometries, we
deliberately span the predicted performance range: a few designs the
surrogate predicts to be \emph{worst}-performing, a few
\emph{mediocre}, and a few \emph{best}-performing are each built in
both material systems. Comparing the measured ordering of the
PLA/TPU specimens against their hollow-aluminum/stainless-steel
counterparts tests whether both systems preserve the same
rank ordering of energy-absorption performance, which would indicate
that the optimization transfers across material systems rather than
overfitting to the printed polymers. We treat this as a
\emph{stringent, exploratory} transfer test rather than a presumed
one-to-one validation: the deformation modes, joint compliance,
friction, pretension behavior, and strain-rate sensitivity all differ
between the PLA/TPU and aluminum/steel systems, so agreement is not
expected a priori. The rank-preservation criterion is fixed in advance
as the Spearman rank-correlation coefficient $\rho_s$ between the two
material systems' orderings of the primary metric (SEA), with peak
transmitted force reported as a secondary ranking; $\rho_s$ near unity
would support cross-system transfer of the learned design ranking.
Table~\ref{tab:metal-validation} reports the planned rank-ordering
comparison and Fig.~\ref{fig:metal-validation} shows the assembled
metal-analog and printed-polymer specimens for each performance tier.

\section{Conclusions}
\label{sec:conclusions}
% =============================================================================

We have presented an experiment-driven Bayesian-optimization framework
for designing multi-material 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired energy
absorbers using PLA struts and TPU tension elements. The framework
parameterizes a family of unit cells, fabricates each candidate on a
single multi-material FDM platform with TPU tendons anchored inside the
PLA strut ends, characterizes the response under
quasi-static compression and drop-weight impact, and updates a
Gaussian-process surrogate~\citep{balandat2020botorch} that recommends
the next batch of designs. \todo{Two-sentence quantitative summary of

replicate prints).} The approach is broadly applicable to architected
absorbers whose constitutive response is difficult to calibrate from
first principles and where physical experiments---rather than
simulations---are the natural ground truth.

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
% Abstract -- JMD requires 150--200 words, Latin characters only (no math),
% structured as background, approach, results, conclusions.
% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{abstract}
Tensegrity-inspired architectures combine rigid compression members with a
continuous network of soft tension elements, yielding lightweight assemblies
with tunable nonlinear responses that are attractive for energy-absorbing
applications such as protective equipment, packaging, and aerospace landing
structures. Multi-material fused-deposition modeling (FDM) of polylactic
acid (PLA) struts and thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) tension elements
makes it possible to fabricate diverse tensegrity-inspired geometries
rapidly enough to support a high-throughput experimental search, while
the rate-dependent damping of TPU is itself an asset for impact mitigation.
We report an experiment-driven Bayesian optimization (BO) framework in
which a Gaussian-process surrogate is trained directly on physical
quasi-static compression and drop-weight impact data and used to
recommend the next batch of designs to print and test. The framework
parameterizes a family of tensegrity-inspired unit cells over strut
geometry, tension-element cross-section, connectivity topology, and
unit-cell tiling, and optimizes peak transmitted force, specific energy
absorption, and compaction efficiency.

\section{Drop-Tower Characterization Notes}
\label{si:drop}
% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
The primary drop fixture is a bungee-assisted laboratory drop tower whose base
accelerates downward faster than \(1g\); unconstrained specimens lift off the
base during descent by design of the rig, so the protocol constrains the
specimen top through light tethers and registers the base. Protocol details,
the accelerometer-tuning campaign, and the impact-window analysis are recorded
in \href{\repo/pull/67}{PR~\#67},
\href{\repo/issues/71}{issue~\#71}, and
\href{\repo/pull/74}{PR~\#74}.

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Metal-Analog Validation Plan}
\label{si:metal-validation}
% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
A final validation campaign rebuilds a subset of the $T_3$-prism designs as
metal analogs---hollow aluminum rods for the compression members and
stainless-steel threaded cables for the tension members---using the same
$R$, $H$, $\theta$, and member-diameter parameterization as the printed
PLA/TPU specimens. To probe transfer across material systems rather than
only confirming the optimum, the selected designs deliberately span the
predicted performance range: representatives the surrogate predicts to be
worst-, mid-, and best-performing are each built in both material systems.
Agreement between the measured PLA/TPU ranking and the
hollow-aluminum/stainless-steel ranking (reported in the main-text
metal-analog validation table and figure) indicates
that the optimization generalizes beyond the as-printed polymers.

\paragraph{Print platform and joint geometry.} The working platform is
a Bambu Lab~H2D printer, which permits a single rigid--soft build
without filament swaps. Strut endpoints are tied to cables through
parametric joint geometries developed and ranked through a five-design

eyelet-loop, and TPU-rebar variants); the working prototype uses a
dovetail joint (Design~B) with an anchor-bulb backup (Design~A) for
sensitivity studies, with a captive TPU core routed inside the PLA
shell to keep the soft tendon protected from layer-line failure at
the strut-to-cable transition. The full five-design comparison and the
selected junction are detailed in the Supplementary Information.\todo{Cite the
joint-design Phase-3 CAD review (Edison ANALYSIS \texttt{19e0c868}) and the

\paragraph{Supports for soft members.} Because near-vertical TPU
tendons are otherwise unsupported during printing, the slicer profile
combines a tensegrity-specific Bambu Studio recipe (support threshold
angle dropped from~40\textdegree{} to~10\textdegree, support material
matched to the rigid extruder) with manually generated narrowing
pillars that ray-cast against the printable mesh underside, producing
TPU-safe coverage of vertical members without slicer-side painting.

Tensegrity structures are assemblies of rigid compression members

remarkable strength-to-weight ratios and tunable nonlinear mechanical

properties have made tensegrity attractive across scales, from
metamaterial unit cells~\citep{amendola2014experimental,
zhang2018tensegrity, fraternali2015tensegrity} to compliant impact-absorbing

under drop-weight impact~\citep{pajunen2019design}, opening a path
toward additively manufactured architected absorbers. Throughout, we use

network of pretensioned soft tension elements---while relaxing the strict
classical requirement that no two compression members touch and that the
tension members behave as ideal inextensible cables; here the tension elements
